nameStory: This delicate damselfly gets its name from the distinctive forked projections at the tip of the male's abdomen, which look like the tines of a tiny fork. The species honors French entomologist Jules Pierre Rambur, who described many dragonfly and damselfly species in the 1800s.
description: Rambur's Forktail is a small, slender damselfly that's part of the narrow-winged damselfly family. Like all damselflies, it holds its wings folded back along its body when at rest, unlike dragonflies which hold theirs outstretched. Males are typically bright green with striking blue segments near the tail end, while females come in more variable colors including orange-red, olive green, or sometimes similar to males. These tiny aerial hunters are delicate creatures, easily recognized by their thin bodies and fluttering flight pattern around water.

idTips.label: Male coloration
idTips.description: Males display a vibrant green body with brilliant blue coloring on the 8th and 9th abdominal segments near the tail - this blue 'cap' catches sunlight beautifully and is visible even from several feet away

idTips.label: Female color variation
idTips.description: Females show remarkable color diversity - some are bright orange-red like tiny flames, others olive green, and some match the male's green and blue pattern

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: When perched, wings fold neatly along the slender body rather than spreading outward, and feel papery-thin if gently touched

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Flies with a weak, fluttering motion close to water surfaces, often landing on emergent vegetation that sways gently under their minimal weight

idTips.label: Forked tail appendages
idTips.description: Males have distinctive fork-like projections at the abdomen tip that are visible with close observation, giving the species its common name

habitat: Look for Rambur's Forktail around still or slow-moving freshwater habitats like ponds, marshes, lake edges, and sluggish streams throughout New England. They prefer areas with abundant emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and water lilies where they can easily perch and hunt for small insects. You'll often spot them in sunny, protected coves and backwater areas where the water warms quickly.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males establishing territories around prime egg-laying sites in shallow, vegetated waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during warm summer months when mating and egg-laying are most common. Look for them during sunny afternoons when they're most active.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall in warmer years, though numbers decrease as temperatures drop and breeding season winds down.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with frost, while eggs and larvae overwinter in pond sediments and among aquatic vegetation, developing slowly until the following year.

funFact: Rambur's Forktail is a true globetrotter - it's the most widespread damselfly in the entire Western Hemisphere, found from Canada all the way down to Chile, and has even island-hopped to Hawaii and the Caribbean, making it one of nature's most successful small-scale colonizers.
confusionNotes: Rambur's Forktail can be tricky to distinguish from other forktail species, but focus on the male's bright blue segments 8 and 9 - Eastern Forktails have blue only on segment 9, while Fragile Forktails are much smaller overall. Memory trick: 'Rambur's got two blue' (segments 8 and 9).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'narrow-winged' damselflies, these insects' wings are actually proportionally quite broad - the name refers to how narrow they appear when folded along the body compared to dragonflies' permanently outstretched wings.
compareHints: Among New England's forktails, Rambur's is distinguished by the male's two blue abdominal segments (8 and 9) versus the Eastern Forktail's single blue segment. The Fragile Forktail is noticeably smaller, while the Lilypad Forktail has more extensive blue coloring. Female Rambur's show the most dramatic color variation of any regional forktail species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's forktails, Eastern Forktails are typically the most common and have the most pronounced fork marking at their tail tip.

Among New England's forktails, the Fragile Forktail's exclamation mark shoulder stripes set it apart from the Eastern Forktail's more linear shoulder markings and the Citrine Forktail's brighter yellow-green coloration.
Among New England's forktails, the Lilypad Forktail is most reliably identified by its strong association with floating vegetation and lily pads.
Among New England's forktails, the Citrine Forktail is distinguished by its bright yellow coloration - Eastern Forktails tend to be more blue-green, while Fragile Forktails are typically orange.
